Cerebras CBRS shares have plunged 25.3% in the past month, underperforming the broader Zacks Business Services sector, which returned 0.3%.

The company's shares have also underperformed its competitors, which include NVIDIA NVDA, Advanced Micro Devices AMD, and Intel INTC in the AI space. Shares of NVIDIA and Advanced Micro Devices gained 1.6% and 9.7%, respectively, while Intel lost 5.6% over the past month.

The underperformance can be attributed to near-term margin pressure from higher costs associated with renting back systems to expand its cloud capacity. Data center availability constraints and deployment delays could limit revenue growth, while significant investments in manufacturing and infrastructure weigh on profitability. Heavy dependence on OpenAI poses customer concentration risks.

CBRS Stock Performance
Zacks Investment Research

Image Source: Zacks Investment Research

However, Cerebras is benefiting from surging demand for high-speed AI inference, expanding cloud deployments and strategic partnerships with hyperscalers. Growing data center capacity, manufacturing expansion and a strong backlog are supporting its long-term growth prospects.

CBRS Benefits From Strong AI Demand and Backlog Growth

Cerebras is benefiting from robust demand for artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure, driven by the rapid adoption of high-speed inference across enterprises, hyperscalers and AI developers. The company's second-quarter 2026 core revenues surged 103% year over year to $209.9 million, reflecting strong demand for its AI computing solutions. Core cloud and other services revenues jumped 287% to $127.7 million, supported by expanding OpenAI deployments and increased cloud customer usage.

The company is aggressively expanding its data center footprint to capitalize on increasing AI infrastructure investments. The company secured more than 600 megawatts of data center capacity, either operational or under contract for delivery by the end of 2027. Its manufacturing expansion initiatives, supported by partnerships with Flex, Sanmina and TSMC, are expected to increase manufacturing capacity by more than tenfold in 2026. These investments position Cerebras to address growing customer demand and accelerate revenue growth.

Strategic collaborations with OpenAI, Amazon Web Services (AWS) and other hyperscalers further strengthen Cerebras' growth prospects. Its partnership with OpenAI is supporting strong demand for high-speed AI inference, while AWS integration through Amazon Bedrock, expected to become generally available in the first quarter of 2027, should expand enterprise adoption. Growing customer engagements across AI coding, agentic workflows and cybersecurity provide additional opportunities to diversify its revenue streams.

Cerebras' strong backlog also supports future upside. Remaining performance obligations stood at $25.4 billion as of June 30, 2026, supporting investments in infrastructure and manufacturing expansion. The company expects core revenues to more than triple in 2027, followed by significant growth in subsequent years. Expanding adoption across AI coding, agentic workflows and cybersecurity applications is expected to strengthen Cerebras' long-term growth trajectory.

title: Will Intel (INTC) Beat Estimates Again in Its Next Earnings Report?
detail:
Will Intel (INTC) Beat Estimates Again in Its Next Earnings Report?
Zacks Equity Research
Fri, October 16, 2026 at 8:10 AM MST 3 min read
INTC
Trade Intel on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Looking for a stock that has been consistently beating earnings estimates and might be well positioned to keep the streak alive in its next quarterly report? Intel (INTC), which belongs to the Zacks Semiconductor - General industry, could be a great candidate to consider.

When looking at the last two reports, this world's largest chipmaker has recorded a strong streak of surpassing earnings estimates. The company has topped estimates by 1,450.00%, on average, in the last two quarters.

For the most recent quarter, Intel was expected to post earnings of $0.21 per share, but it reported $0.42 per share instead, representing a surprise of 100.00%. For the previous quarter, the consensus estimate was $0.01 per share, while it actually produced $0.29 per share, a surprise of 2,800.00%.

Price and EPS Surprise

For Intel, estimates have been trending higher, thanks in part to this earnings surprise history. And when you look at the stock's positive Zacks Earnings ESP (Expected Surprise Prediction), it's a great indicator of a future earnings beat, especially when combined with its solid Zacks Rank.

Our research shows that stocks with the combination of a positive Earnings ESP and a Zacks Rank #3 (Hold) or better produce a positive surprise nearly 70% of the time. In other words, if you have 10 stocks with this combination, the number of stocks that beat the consensus estimate could be as high as seven.

The Zacks Earnings ESP compares the Most Accurate Estimate to the Zacks Consensus Estimate for the quarter; the Most Accurate Estimate is a version of the Zacks Consensus whose definition is related to change. The idea here is that analysts revising their estimates right before an earnings release have the latest information, which could potentially be more accurate than what they and others contributing to the consensus had predicted earlier.

Intel currently has an Earnings ESP of +1.11%, which suggests that analysts have recently become bullish on the company's earnings prospects. This positive Earnings ESP when combined with the stock's Zacks Rank #3 (Hold) indicates that another beat is possibly around the corner. We expect the company's next earnings report to be released on October 29, 2026.

When the Earnings ESP comes up negative, investors should note that this will reduce the predictive power of the metric. But, a negative value is not indicative of a stock's earnings miss.

Many companies end up beating the consensus EPS estimate, though this is not the only reason why their shares gain. Additionally, some stocks may remain stable even if they end up missing the consensus estimate.

Heading into the decline, Intel has improving results. Intel's latest quarterly report posted what CEO Lip-Bu Tan called "our strongest revenue growth in more than fifteen years." That same report showed its foundry business posting a large operating loss, a reminder of how costly its manufacturing push remains.

Data center chips anchor Intel's AI business, with Xeon server processors handling cloud, enterprise and AI infrastructure workloads. Beyond servers, Intel has also demonstrated rack-scale AI systems with SambaNova and Foxconn for inference and agentic AI tasks. Its Client Computing and Physical AI Group adds processors for PCs, edge AI and robotics.

Intel's Foundry Push Sets It Apart

Contract manufacturing is what separates Intel from its biggest rivals. Intel designs chips and is building a contract manufacturing business that requires heavy spending, grounded by process technologies such as Intel 3 and Intel 18A. Rivals AMD and NVIDIA design chips and outsource production, which leaves the cost of building factories to their manufacturing partners.

Spending plans at Intel reflect that commitment. The company is increasing investment in equipment, clean room space and substrates, and it's expanding capacity for Xeon processors built on Intel 3. Washington backs that effort too, with Intel receiving U.S. CHIPS Act funding that supports its domestic production.

AMD built its AI franchise on an outsourced production model. Its Data Center lineup includes EPYC server processors, Instinct accelerators and Helios rack-scale systems, and that division now generates the majority of AMD revenue. Anthropic plans to deploy MI450 Series GPUs in Helios racks, while other large AI customers are scaling Instinct deployments.

Beyond the data center, Ryzen processors lifted AMD client sales, and embedded demand strengthened across several end markets. On the gaming side, AMD's business shrank over the same stretch, leaving the company more dependent on AI and server demand.

Weighing Intel's Bull and Bear Cases

Intel's revenue recovery drives the optimistic view, with the company reporting this result: Data center and foundry sales both grew in the latest quarter, while client computing also expanded. Intel's gross margin improved sharply from a year earlier as well, giving the turnaround a stronger financial base.

Foundry spending is the main worry for Intel. Its foundry unit is still running a large operating loss.

Strong AI growth stories at Intel and AMD sit alongside real near-term pressure from the rotation. On balance, Intel brings a recovering business with heavy capital needs, while AMD offers a lighter production model tied closely to AI accelerator demand. Shareholders of these chip stocks, especially INTC, should consider keeping their position sizes modest until the foundry question at Intel settles.

The biggest names took the heaviest hits. Intel has lost more than 20% in two weeks, while AMD dropped over 5% intraday on October 14.

Why Are Investors Dumping the AI Boom's Favorite Chip Stocks?

AI spending doubts. OpenAI reportedly told investors its annualized revenue neared $50 billion, short of earlier $70 billion estimates. Broadcom CEO Hock Tan has also described some AI investors as gamblers.

Inflation and rate hikes. September consumer prices rose 3.7% year over year, topping forecasts. Traders now price a 92% chance of another Fed hike this year.

Asian memory rout. Selling spread from Korea's chip-heavy KOSPI. Meanwhile, progress by Chinese memory maker ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT) fueled fears that China is catching up.

Demand, however, is not the problem. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC) reported a 68.7% jump in third-quarter profit, yet its US shares still fell 1.8%.

Can Buyers Defend the $500 Zone?

On the daily chart, SOXX trades below its 50-day moving average (MA), which capped rallies in August and September (red arrows). The Relative Strength Index (RSI), a momentum gauge, has fallen to 36, its lowest reading since July.

Thursday's volume spike suggests dip buyers are stepping in. If selling resumes, the 0.5 Fibonacci retracement near $481 is the next major support.

SOXX daily chart / Source: Tradingview

Overhead, SOXX must reclaim $523 and the 50-day MA near $540. The bigger barrier sits at $573, the 0.236 Fibonacci level.

UBS reads the sell-off as a reset:

"More of a recalibration of expectations than a fundamental break in the AI investment story."

JPMorgan strategists also flagged a possible inflection point. Yet Big Tech plans roughly $800 billion in capital spending this year, per Goldman Sachs. The next leg for chips may hinge on borrowing costs, not demand.

title: Is AMD Stock Safer Or Riskier Than A Year Ago?

Investors holding Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) stock have enjoyed a very good year: shares returned 157.8% over the past year, compared with a 17.9% gain for the S&P 500. A return of that magnitude prompts a closer look at the underlying business, and the company's financial report for the quarter ended June 27, 2026, provides the latest view into its accounts. Has the company taken on more risk to get there?

Mostly Safer, But AMD Is Spending More On Assets

The balance sheet is mostly safer, because AMD holds far more cash than it did a year ago. At the end of the quarter on June 27, 2026, cash and short-term investments stood at $13.1 billion, up from $5.87 billion a year earlier. Total debt also rose during that period, climbing to $4.28 billion from $3.89 billion. Even so, AMD ended the quarter with net cash of $8.84 billion.

AMD has changed in one key area: capital spending is now running above its depreciation and amortization charge. Over the twelve months to June 27, 2026, capital spending reached $1.68 billion, compared with a $1.17 billion depreciation and amortization charge. That reverses a long trend. At each of the 16 quarter ends prior to that, from June 2022 to March 2026, twelve-month capital spending stayed below the charge for the same twelve months. In the latest quarter alone, AMD spent $808 million on new assets, up from $282 million in the same quarter a year earlier.

Why Is AMD Spending More Now?

The company appears to be spending to keep pace with demand it did not anticipate. Server chip supply ran tight through the first half of the year because much of the demand was unforecasted, management noted on the August 4, 2026, call. AMD has also been working across its supply chain, from wafers to substrates, to raise capacity for servers.

That demand is visible in the latest financial results. Data center revenue grew 107% from a year earlier to $6.7 billion in fiscal Q2 2026, management said. Helios, the system housing AMD's MI450 series GPUs, was in production at the time of the call, with Microsoft and Anthropic both planning to deploy it. First shipments were scheduled to begin later that quarter, which is the period AMD reports next, on or around November 3, 2026.

What Does AMD's Spending Mean For Your Money?

Free cash flow, the cash remaining after capital spending, was $1.56 billion in fiscal Q2 2026. Over the twelve months to June 27, capital spending amounted to 16.6% of the cash AMD's operations brought in. This offers a positive signal for shareholders: AMD pays for its new assets out of a small portion of its cash and keeps the rest.

Marvell Technology is poised for phenomenal growth over the next five years

Though the CEOs of Broadcom and Intel expressed concerns about the availability of capital to fund infrastructure expansion amid a high-interest-rate environment, they remained bullish about the state of AI. Broadcom's Tan, for example, pointed out that AI compute demand is outpacing supply, and he expects the supply constraints to persist through 2030.

Marvell Technology is gradually becoming a key player in the AI chip space. Though it trails Broadcom in the market for custom AI processors and networking chips, Marvell's recent investor day presentation makes it quite clear that it is going to make a big name for itself in the semiconductor industry.

The custom AI chips that Marvell manufactures help hyperscalers and AI companies lower operating costs. For instance, Microsoft claims that its latest custom AI chip is 40% more efficient compared to graphics processing unit (GPU)-based systems. Other estimates suggest that custom AI processors could reduce inference costs by 40% to 60% compared to GPUs.
